title: Four ways a broken Factur-X invoice stays green in veraPDF and Mustang
summary: Validation tools veraPDF and Mustang fail to catch four specific configuration errors in Factur-X invoices, including incorrect /AFRelationship values that popular libraries set by default. The issue highlights that validators answer different questions than invoice compliance specs require, creating security gaps when wrong values are the library defaults.
content:
Our release gate for Factur-X/ZUGFeRD hybrids used to end the way most do: veraPDF says the PDF/A-3 is compliant, Mustang says the invoice is valid, ship it. Then we started breaking our own files on purpose, and four of the breaks sailed through green. This post is the list of those four, with the exact checks that close them. Most of it got hashed out in public, in a SolidInvoice issue where several people building generators compared notes — worth reading if you want the raw exchange: https://github.com/SolidInvoice/SolidInvoice/issues/1439
A hybrid invoice is a PDF/A-3 with the invoice XML embedded as factur-x.xml. Every embedded file referenced from the document's /AF array carries an /AFRelationship key, and the Factur-X / ZUGFeRD spec cares about its value: Alternative for BASIC, EN 16931 and EXTENDED profiles as used in Germany, Data for MINIMUM and BASIC WL.
Take a known-good EN 16931 hybrid that both validators pass, and flip only that key:
import pikepdf

pdf = pikepdf.open("good-en16931.pdf")
pdf.Root.AF[0].AFRelationship = pikepdf.Name("/Data")  # was /Alternative
pdf.save("flipped.pdf")

Re-run the gate on flipped.pdf:
veraPDF (1.31.167 local install; same result re-run in the verapdf/cli Docker image, 1.30.2): still isCompliant="true". Nothing wrong with that — /AFRelationship semantics are Factur-X domain, not PDF/A conformance. veraPDF is answering a different question than the one you think you asked.
Mustangproject 2.26.0, --action validate: still <summary status="valid"/>. The notices it did print on our file were unrelated content rules.
So the one key the spec makes profile-dependent is exactly the key neither tool will fail on. It gets better: the wrong value is the default outcome in popular libraries. Python's factur-x (akretion) defaults the attachment to afrelationship="data" in both generate functions, overridable via a parameter; horstoeko/zugferd in PHP has the same pattern. If you never set it explicitly, you ship Data on an EN 16931 i

zh.summary: 验证工具veraPDF和Mustang无法捕获Factur-X发票中的四个特定配置错误，包括流行库默认设置的不正确/AFRelationship值。该问题突出了验证器回答的问题与发票合规规范要求的问题不同，当错误值是库的默认值时，就会产生安全漏洞。

title: Questioning the medtech "partner program" — when a broker is just a broker
summary: Medtech 'partner program' brokers can shift supplier qualification accountability from themselves to manufacturers through managed supplier contracts, creating hidden QMS compliance liability for small manufacturers. The risk intensifies with 'summa form' variants that provide minimal audit trails, placing regulatory responsibility on manufacturers for suppliers they never directly vetted.
content:
The pitch always sounds reasonable. A "partner program" promises vetted suppliers, shared audits, pre-negotiated terms, and faster onboarding. From a CMO perspective, that should be music. We sit on 40+ active suppliers, and the cost of qualifying a new sterilization partner is measured in months, not weeks. So when a broker approached us last year waving a curated network of "audited" medtech suppliers, I sat up. Then I read the contract. Then I asked questions. Then I started writing this down.
This is not a screed against partnership models. Some are genuinely useful. But a few of them are repackaged brokerages dressed in risk-sharing language, and the rosy rhetoric hides a real shift in who carries the QMS accountability. If you are a small manufacturer — two QA people, mounting CAPA backlog, next notified body visit in eight months — that shift can break you quietly.
In medtech, a partner program is usually one of three things:
A referral network — a broker introduces you to suppliers they have not audited, and disappears.
A managed supplier program — the broker claims ongoing qualification, monitoring, and re-audit on your behalf, often for a fee layered on each PO.
A license/white-label arrangement — the broker lets you resell or co-brand product from an OEM whose own QMS you do not see.
The middle one is the one with the most interesting compliance teeth. Because if a managed supplier program fails, the question your auditor will ask is not "did the broker do its job?" — it is "did you control your supplier?" That question lands on the legal manufacturer, not the broker.
I have also seen a fourth, quieter variant: a programme that on paper is managed, but in practice the broker sends you a one-page "summa form" — summa meaning "merely" or "just for show" in Tamil — to confirm supplier status, and calls that qualification. The form is the entire audit trail. That is the version to watch for.
I sat in a CAPA review where a non-conformance had travelled through

zh.title: 质疑医疗科技"合作伙伴计划"——当经纪人只是经纪人时
zh.summary: 医疗科技"合作伙伴计划"经纪人可以通过托管供应商合同将供应商资格认证责任从自身转移给制造商，为小型制造商造成隐藏的QMS合规责任。通过提供最少审计跟踪的"summa form"变体，风险加剧，使制造商对从未直接审查过的供应商承担监管责任。

title: I Built an AI Tutor That Cannot Do the Homework
summary: A parent built an AI tutor that is architecturally prevented from solving homework by isolating correct answers from the language model layer entirely, with prompts designed to always end in a guiding question. The structural approach ensures the tutor guides understanding rather than enabling shortcuts, and prevents jailbreaking through code enforcement rather than policy.
content:
My son is nine, in second grade, and has ADHD. He can calculate, but store-bought trainer apps reward taps, not understanding, and he finishes each one in an evening by guessing. So I built our own tutor around his actual school textbook (the skin is a space school: missions follow the Apollo 11 route, 15 rockets in the collection), and the whole architecture serves a single ban: the LLM is not allowed to solve the task.
Most AI homework helpers on the market do the homework. Mine can't, and not because of a polite system prompt. The design is structural, not polite:
The mentor endpoint receives only the task text. The correct answers live in a table the LLM layer never reads, so there's nothing to leak and nowhere to jailbreak.
The prompt must end every reply with one question that moves the child forward. No final answers, no "the answer is".
The similar-example mode works through an analogous problem with different numbers. It may name that example's answer, never the original task's.
If you take one thing from my story: isolate the answer from the model, then design the prompt around a question-ending rule. Bans you can verify in code beat bans you can only write in prose. I trust the first kind.
## Content pipeline: the textbook is the source of truth
Homework comes from a specific textbook, so the dataset has to match it verbatim: our numbering, our wording, so the notebook can be shown to the teacher in the morning. I forbid generative paraphrase, and the pipeline enforces it:
page scan (PNG, 300 dpi)
-> vision model with a narrow prompt: "transcribe task N verbatim"
-> second pass on disputed fragments
-> verification against the scan; the scan always wins
-> a card in the dataset
Full-page transcription by vision models is unstable. Narrow one-task prompts are reliable, so my pipeline reads pages piece by piece.
Why am I so paranoid? Here's a real catch from the first weeks: an external agent prepared five tasks for a page, and verification against the scan

zh.title: 我构建了一个无法做作业的AI家教

title: What Building Redis, Git and an LLM From Scratch Taught Us About Using Them
summary: The build-your-own-x tutorial collection helps engineers understand foundational technologies like Redis, Git, and LLMs by rebuilding simplified versions, turning abstract concepts into concrete understanding. The approach enables cheaper junior onboarding, better contractor vetting, and more informed technical decisions.
content:
There is a GitHub repository with about 550,000 stars called build-your-own-x. It is not a library. It is a curated catalog of step-by-step tutorials where people rebuild the technologies we all use daily: a SQLite clone in C, Redis in C++ or Python, a container in a hundred lines of Go, git from the inside, a vector search engine, even a small GPT. CC0 licensed, started by Daniel Stefanovic, maintained by CodeCrafters.
Take Redis. You use it for cache and queues. Then you spend an evening on a mini-Redis tutorial and the wire protocol stops being abstract:
*2
$3
GET
$3
key

That is a GET command on the RESP protocol. Once you have parsed one with your own code, connection pool behavior, timeouts and persistence settings turn from copied flags into decisions. Same shift happens with B+trees after you build a storage engine page by page: EXPLAIN output starts reading like a sentence.
We do not read it cover to cover. We pull a tutorial when a task needs a fast prototype or a mental model:
RAG and agents. LLMs from scratch and Karpathy's Zero to Hero cover tokens, embeddings, attention. Chunking and retrieval choices stop being folklore.
Search and semantics. The vector space indexing engine and TF-IDF tutorials are the shortest path from TF-IDF to BM25 to embeddings, which is exactly the line search engines followed and the line LLMs read your site along today.
Slow e-commerce queries. Let's Build a Simple Database teaches indexes and transactions from the inside.
Front end. Build your own React explains where render time actually goes, which matters in headless setups.
## The part that is not about code
Three effects we can put a business value on:
Juniors level up cheaper. Assign a "build X" section matching your stack, and framework knowledge turns into platform understanding. You notice it in code review.
Contractor vetting. Ask a candidate to explain what happens between a button press and data landing in the CRM. People who built a web server or a database answ

zh.summary: 自己动手构建教程集合通过重建简化版本帮助工程师理解Redis、Git和LLM等基础技术，将抽象概念转化为具体理解。这种方法可以降低初级工程师培训成本、更好地评估承包商，以及做出更明智的技术决策。

title: Show DEV: 25 free Chinese learning tools with no backend, and the honest traffic numbers
summary: A developer built a free static HTML Chinese learning site with 25 resource pages and saw initial traction of 93 page views in eight days, with notable traffic from ChatGPT share links. The project demonstrates that content-focused sites without backends or backlinks can still reach learners, particularly mobile users across multiple countries.
content:
I built this because I couldn't find a free place to practice the boring parts of Chinese. Typing tones. Getting stroke order right. Knowing which measure word goes with which noun.
It's 46 pages now, and 25 of those are tools or resource pages. The pinyin chart is the one people use most. The stroke order page animates each character. There's a transport simulator that runs real airport and subway conversations, plus a hospital one, because those are the two situations where I froze hardest.
All of it is static HTML, CSS, and vanilla JS. No backend, no database, no login page. The audio is the browser's own speech synthesis. I call it that instead of dressing it up as an AI tutor.
How the traffic looks
Eight days of Cloudflare data: 93 page views, 71 sessions, 66 of them real humans once I strip the bots. About one visit in nine came from a search engine. Zero backlinks.
That last number is the one that matters and it's the one I can't buy.
Ranking on Google is out of reach from where I build, so I'm working Bing, which is maybe a tenth of the English market. What gets indexed, gets indexed slowly.
One thing did catch me off guard. A ChatGPT share link turned up as a referrer. Somebody pasted a page into a conversation and clicked through. It's nofollow, so it earns no ranking credit, but it means the content is reaching people somehow.
Three weeks in, mobile was at 50% of sessions for a day. Four countries, all phones.
People learn Chinese on the bus, not at a desk.
What's next
If you've run a domain with no backlinks and no traffic, I'd like to hear what moved the needle for you.

title: Stop Searching Your Documents Manually: Build Your Own AI Knowledge Base with n8n, Gemini, and Qdrant
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) solves the word-matching problem that limits basic search and generic language models by retrieving relevant document passages before generating answers. Building RAG on infrastructure you control with tools like n8n, Gemini, and Qdrant is cheaper than subscription knowledge bases and avoids the plausibility-hallucination problem of LLMs answering from internal knowledge.
content:
Every growing company hits the same wall eventually. Someone asks a question in Slack that’s already been answered in a PDF from eight months ago, or buried in a page of documentation nobody remembers writing. The information exists. It’s just scattered across enough files that finding it takes longer than re-deriving the answer from scratch.
The usual fix is a paid knowledge base tool with per-seat pricing that scales badly the moment a team grows past a handful of people. There’s a cheaper path that gets less attention: build your own retrieval system on infrastructure you already control, using automation software instead of a subscription product.
A basic search bar handles small document collections fine. Ten files, no problem. A hundred files, and it starts missing things constantly, not because the answer isn’t there, but because the words don’t match. Someone writes “customer churn” in a report and a colleague searches for “client retention” six months later and gets nothing, even though the paragraph they need is sitting three documents down.
Chat tools built on top of a general-purpose language model don’t fully solve this either. Ask one a question about your internal process and it will either admit it has no idea or, worse, generate something plausible-sounding that has nothing to do with how your company actually operates. Neither failure mode is acceptable when someone is relying on the answer to do their job correctly.
This is the gap that retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG, is built to close. Instead of asking a model to answer from memory, you first search a database of your own content for the passages most relevant to the question, then hand those passages to the model along with the question itself. The model still writes the answer, but it’s writing from material it was just shown rather than guessing.
Making RAG useful requires more than picking a vector database and calling it done. Content has to be pulled in from where

zh.title: 停止手动搜索文档：使用 n8n、Gemini 和 Qdrant 构建自己的 AI 知识库
zh.summary: 检索增强生成 (RAG) 通过在生成答案前检索相关文档段落，解决了限制基础搜索和通用语言模型的词匹配问题。使用 n8n、Gemini 和 Qdrant 等工具在自己控制的基础设施上构建 RAG，成本低于订阅知识库，并避免了 LLM 从内部知识生成答案时的似是而非的幻觉问题。

title: Why Apple Rewrote Full Disk Access for AI Agents: Permission Is a Lease, Judgment Is per Action
summary: Apple's October 2026 Full Disk Access controls require explicit user action to prevent AI agents from exposing entire system contents without user knowledge. Apple's three-layer model distinguishes install-time capability leases, class-level re-consent when apps shift to agent behavior, and per-action judgment to evaluate whether specific read operations should proceed.
content:
Why Apple Rewrote Full Disk Access for AI Agents: Permission Is a Lease, Judgment Is per Action


On October 2, 2026, Apple announced "additional controls" for macOS Full Disk Access — going forward it can only be granted with "very explicit user action." Apple's verbatim reason: "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems — including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history — without users' full knowledge and understanding."
The reported trigger: Inc. columnist Jason Aten said Meta's Muse agent surfaced Apple Messages content without that scope; Meta disputed it (TechCrunch via intelligibberish, Oct 3). Apple gave no rollout date. Late 2025, Microsoft did the same thing on Windows 11 (reversed Agent Workspace's default folder access after backlash).
One line from the autonainews write-up names the whole failure mode:
An app abusing broad access doesn't necessarily do anything that exceeds what it was authorised to do — it just does more of it, or more sensitive versions of it, than a user would have agreed to if asked directly.
Apple's fix detects the behavior class — a shift toward autonomous agent behavior triggers re-authorization — and re-asks. That's a consent upgrade. But after the user re-taps "Allow," the 3 a.m. sweep of ~/Documents + the Messages DB + browsing history still passes every check, because every read is still technically authorized. Apple detects the class; nobody scores the instance.
The three layers:
Capability lease — may this app ever touch the disk? Binary, install-time, persists indefinitely.
Class-level re-consent — is it an app or an agent now? Apple's Oct 2 notice.
Per-action judgment — should this action, right now, fire? Not shipped. This is what I built below.
Scored against the live decision gate at https://scriptmasterlabs.com/api/harness/decide (local-heuristic-v1, bands ≥0.80 auto / 0.50–0.79 confirm / <0.50 escalate), October 5, 2026 ~09:31 EDT:

zh.title: 为什么 Apple 为 AI 代理重写了完全磁盘访问：权限是租约，判断针对每个操作
zh.summary: Apple 2026 年 10 月的完全磁盘访问控制要求用户采取明确操作，以防止 AI 代理在未经用户知情的情况下暴露整个系统内容。Apple 的三层模型区分了安装时的能力租约、应用转向代理行为时的类级重新同意，以及用于评估是否应该进行特定读取操作的每个操作判断。

title: What I Learned Building Backend Features Used Across Multiple Clients
summary: Backend APIs consumed by multiple clients with different versions must plan for backward compatibility during development, not after, because technically correct changes can still break older clients in production. Introducing new optional fields and migrating existing records before requiring new schemas allows clients to transition without forcing simultaneous updates.
content:
When engineers are early in their careers, we often think that if an API is correct, tested, and returns the expected response, the feature is ready.
Working on production systems used by different clients changed this perspective.
Backend changes rarely exist in isolation; the same API can be consumed by web, mobile apps, internal servers, etc. This means a backend change can be technically correct and still break the product if it’s not well planned.
Over the years, I learned to think beyond the endpoint/query/mutation itself. Before any changes to an API, I like to ask, “Who consumes this data today?” “How can this be backward compatible so as not to break anything in production?”
An API contract isn't just the route, request body, and response documented in the specification.
Clients can depend on details that may look insignificant from the backend perspective.
For example, imagine an API returning:
{
  "id": "123",
  "role": "speaker"
}

A new requirement allows a user to have multiple roles. From a data-model perspective, changing the response to this might seem natural:
{
  "id": "123",
  "roles": ["speaker", "moderator"]
}

The new model may be better, but replacing role with roles immediately creates a breaking change.
The web application may already support the new model while an older mobile version still expects role.
The backend therefore has to consider not only what the ideal API should look like, but how clients will transition to it.
Deploying a breaking change to production can affect existing clients and users. For that reason, backward compatibility should be considered during development rather than after the feature is ready to be released.
Depending on the situation, one approach is to introduce new data as optional first and migrate existing records before making it mandatory.
One example I would like to share comes from a feature I developed around speaker roles. The new requirement was that every speaker should have a role assigned, which

zh.title: 我在为多个客户端构建后端功能时学到的东西
zh.summary: 被具有不同版本的多个客户端使用的后端 API 必须在开发期间计划向后兼容性，而不是之后，因为技术上正确的更改在生产中仍然可能破坏较旧的客户端。在需要新模式之前引入新的可选字段和迁移现有记录，允许客户端在不强制同时更新的情况下进行转换。

title: pwsh vs Windows PowerShell 5.1: When “Just Install 7” Isn’t Allowed
summary: When Windows PowerShell 5.1 is the corporate floor because of GPO policies, vendor runbooks, or constrained endpoints that block sideloading, writing code for that constraint is better than promoting incompatible 7-only syntax. The comparison provides decision rules for when 5.1 is the right choice and emphasizes documenting the edition and testing module compatibility against the lower bound.
content:
The internet’s favorite PowerShell answer is still: “Install PowerShell 7.” Good advice—when you control the machine. This comparison is for the other universe: corporates, customers, and classrooms where Windows PowerShell 5.1 is the floor and pwsh is a request sitting in someone else’s backlog.

The table is incomplete on purpose. Operators don’t need trivia—they need decision rules.
GPO / golden images pin 5.1 as the admin automation surface.
Vendor runbooks still say powershell.exe and mean 5.1.
Constrained endpoints block sideloading runtimes.
You’re teaching someone whose first production script will be reviewed by a team that only runs 5.1 in CI.
Writing 7-only syntax into that world isn’t modern. It’s inconsiderate.
You need cross-platform scripts for mixed fleets.
You’re hitting encoding pain repeatedly in log pipelines.
You depend on modules or language features that aren’t backported.
Local dev can run 7 while CI validates 5.1—if you consciously design for the lower bound or split editions.
Know which binary ran. powershell.exe vs pwsh.exe. Profiles differ. $PSVersionTable is not optional.
Prefer compatible patterns when targeting unknown machines: classic if over ternary, careful with newer operators.
Test module imports on 5.1 before you document them for helpdesk.
Don’t assume JSON / UTF-8 behavior is identical. Prove it with a fixture file.
Document the edition in the README like you would docume

title: Clef e Clef Flash: modelli open-weights per decisioni rapide (e perché interessano anche il frontend)
summary: Clef and Clef Flash are open-weight decision models optimized for structured outputs (probabilities, scores, constrained choices) rather than generative text, making them better suited for UI components and real-time workflows. Classification models solve the problem of general LLMs derailing into off-topic explanations and format violations when asked to make quick, binary, or scored decisions.
content:
Probabilità al posto di testo, latenze più basse e supporto immagini: una nuova strada per classificazione e triage in tempo reale.
Nel frontend moderno stiamo vedendo una spinta costante verso esperienze più interattive e “assistite”: controlli di qualità, moderazione, triage, suggerimenti contestuali, validazioni intelligenti, scoring di rischio. Il problema? Se per ogni micro-decisione chiami un LLM generativo, ti ritrovi con latenze alte, output poco vincolabili e comportamenti non sempre prevedibili.
Qui entra in gioco una categoria diversa: i decision / classification models. In questa famiglia si inseriscono Clef e Clef Flash, due modelli open-weights progettati per dare risposte strutturate e veloci, più vicine a ciò che serve davvero in UI e workflow operativi.
Clef arriva in due varianti:
Clef (base): modello più grande, pensato per massimizzare accuratezza.
Clef Flash: modello più piccolo (circa 9B parametri), con un obiettivo dichiarato: abbassare drasticamente la latenza anche a costo di un filo di accuratezza.
Il punto non è soltanto “un modello nuovo”, ma il tipo di output: questi modelli sono ottimizzati per produrre probabilità e decisioni vincolate, invece di generare testo libero token per token.
Per chi costruisce interfacce, questa differenza è enorme: significa poter implementare componenti UI che consumano valori numerici stabili (score, confidence, classi) senza dover fare parsing fragile di testo.
Un LLM classico eccelle nel generare testo, ma quando gli chiedi:
“Scegli tra 4 categorie”

title: Realtime Optimistic Updates and WebRTC Reconciliation for Consultation Session Failures
summary: This article examines how to architect video consultation systems to distinguish between ephemeral interface state (cursors, typing indicators) and critical clinical state (consent, notes) when applying optimistic updates over WebRTC. Only ephemeral state should update optimistically; durable clinical decisions require server confirmation to maintain trust boundaries.
content:
Short answer: a video consultation room should apply optimistic updates only to reversible interface state, tag every mutation with a scoped session token and idempotency key, and reconcile against an authoritative room log after any disconnect. WebRTC can carry low-latency presence and cursor traffic, but it should not turn an unconfirmed clinical action into a fact. The uncomfortable trade-off is deliberate: cursors may briefly jump after reconnection; consent, appointment status, and clinician notes must never be guessed.
This is a trust-boundary problem disguised as a latency problem. A patient can reasonably trust the local mute icon to react at once. They cannot reasonably be told that consent was recorded merely because one browser changed color. The architecture has to distinguish those two promises before anyone chooses a transport.
Start by dividing room state into three classes. Ephemeral state includes pointer position, typing indicators, raised-hand animations, and the selection range in a shared note editor. Session state includes participant presence, active speaker, device status, and the current presenter. Durable clinical state includes consent, finalized notes, prescriptions, recording authorization, and appointment disposition. Those classes can share a screen, but they should not share a confirmation rule.
An optimistic cursor update can render locally, receive a monotonically increasing client sequence number, and travel over an RTCDataChannel. On reconnect, the client discards cursor messages older than the latest accepted sequence for that participant. Losing one intermediate coordinate is harmless because a newer coordinate replaces it. A finalized note is different: it needs an idempotent command to an authoritative service, a durable acknowledgement, and a server-assigned revision that every client can reconcile. If the acknowledgement is missing, the interface must show pending or unknown rather than success.
Keep that distinction blunt.

title: California Bans AI 'Robo Bosses': First-in-Nation Law Requires a Human Hand in Firing Decisions
summary: California's SB 947 prohibits employers from using AI algorithms alone to terminate or discipline employees, requiring human corroboration with additional evidence and worker notification. The law takes effect in July 2027 and reflects growing concerns about algorithmic decision-making in employment.
content:
California Bans AI 'Robo Bosses': First-in-Nation Law Requires a Human Hand in Firing Decisions


The next time an algorithm decides a worker deserves to be fired in California, a human being will have to look that decision in the eye — and back it up with evidence. Governor Gavin Newsom on Wednesday signed SB 947, the "No Robo Bosses Act of 2026," making California the first state in the nation to prohibit employers from relying solely on AI-powered automated decision systems to discipline or terminate employees.
The signing caps a remarkable reversal for the legislation. Newsom vetoed an earlier version of the bill just last year, even after it cleared both chambers of the state legislature with broad support, citing concerns that vague notice requirements could chill the adoption of beneficial workplace technologies. The version that reached his desk this time was narrowed to win his approval — and landed amid record public distrust of AI's growing role in the workplace, according to a May survey by the nonprofit United for Respect, which found workers at major retailers increasingly worried that HR decisions are being automated.
At its core, SB 947 establishes a "human-in-the-loop" mandate for the most consequential employment decisions. Employers cannot rely exclusively on an automated decision system when disciplining or firing a worker. Crucially, the law goes further than requiring a rubber stamp: a human reviewer must corroborate the machine's recommendation using additional information such as managerial evaluations, peer reviews, or personnel records.
Transparency is the second pillar. Workers subject to such decisions must be told in writing that AI played a primary role, informed of what personal data the system drew upon, and given the name of a human contact who can walk them through the outcome. title: Eight broken tool calls: how six agent frameworks recover
summary: Testing six AI agent frameworks against eight tool-call failure modes reveals that most recover within two LLM calls, though some like langgraph and OpenAI agents fail on specific error types. Framework design significantly impacts system resilience when models generate malformed requests.
content:
Models send bad tool calls: malformed JSON, a tool name that does not exist, a missing argument. What happens next is decided by the agent framework, not the model. In agentic-arena I measure that directly.
The resilience arena feeds eight scripted faults to every framework. The scripted model turns are byte-identical for all of them, so any difference in outcome is the framework's own error handling:
res-01 calculator called with malformed JSON arguments
res-02 a tool that does not exist
res-03 an unevaluable expression (the tool returns ERROR)
res-04 a required argument missing entirely
res-05 an extra argument the tool does not accept
res-06 search with an empty query
res-07 an expression the safe evaluator must refuse
res-08 arguments serialised as JSON null instead of an object

smolagents

but 6 LLM calls on four faults, against 2 elsewhere



The smolagents split is exact. On the four faults where the tool ran and returned something, it recovers in two calls like everyone else. On the four its validation layer rejects first (unknown name, missing argument, unexpected argument, null arguments), the error never reaches the transcript. The model cannot see it, re-emits the identical call, and the run spends the whole six-call budget, about 2.7x the prompt tokens, with zero tool calls recorded. It still reaches the right final answer, so the item passes. A retry wrapper would not help: the prompt is byte-identical every time.
Google ADK is the only framework that loses both res-01 and res-02. Both are uncaught exceptions rather than the model giving up, which is at least loud, and the kind of failure a retry wrapper can handle.

title: RocketMQ-Rust: route discovery is only the first connectivity check
summary: A RocketMQ architectural note explains that successful route discovery from NameServer only confirms the lookup service works, not that clients can reach the advertised broker. Debugging connectivity requires separate verification of broker reachability and write readiness.
content:
A small debugging note from RocketMQ-Rust’s architecture docs:
NameServer returns topic routes: Broker addresses and queue metadata. In a direct-client deployment, producers and consumers then communicate with the Broker. Message storage and delivery belong to the Broker.
That distinction matters when a client can fetch a route but still cannot send or consume. A successful NameServer request only confirms discovery worked. It does not prove the advertised Broker address is reachable from that client, or that the Broker can accept writes.
A useful first check: compare the Broker address returned in the route with the network the client actually runs in. Then investigate Broker connectivity and write readiness separately.
The architecture documentation explains these boundaries.
Disclosure: This post was generated with AI assistance and checked against the project documentation.

Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend Submission 🤝
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend.
My friend saves everything as a screenshot.
A restaurant they want to try. A product they might buy. A tweet worth rereading. A design idea. A technical explanation. A recommendation somebody sent them.
At the moment they save it, the screenshot feels useful.
A week later, it is just image number 6,842 in the camera roll.
That was the problem I wanted to solve this weekend.
I built Screenshot Graveyard, a tiny memory layer for screenshots.
You drop in screenshots. It reads what is actually visible, turns each image into a compact memory of what it is and why you probably saved it, and stores that memory alongside the original screenshot in the browser.
Later you can ask something vague like:
what was that private access thing I saved?
You do not need the filename. You do not need the exact title. You do not even need to remember the proper noun.
Screenshot Graveyard searches the recovered memories, finds the likely match, and brings the original screenshot back up.
That is the whole product.
I deliberately kept it narrow because the useful moment is not “AI organized my photos.”
It is:
I remembered the idea, but not enough of it to find the screenshot — and the app found it anyway.
The friend I built it for is real, but I am keeping them anonymous. Their screenshot habit is the product brief.
Live app:
https://screenshot-graveyard.vercel.app
Try this flow:
Drop in a few screenshots.
Let Screenshot Graveyard recover a memory for each one.
Search with a fuzzy description instead of the exact words in the screenshot.
Open the result and confirm it surfaced the original image.
The archive itself lives in the browser using IndexedDB.
There is no account and no server-side screenshot library.

title: How I Set Up Encrypted Off-Site Backups for My MacBook With restic and Backblaze B2
summary: A practical guide to setting up automated encrypted backups using restic, Backblaze B2, and Healthchecks.io for cross-platform compatibility and end-to-end encryption. The setup backs up machines daily with data encrypted before leaving the local machine.
content:
Originally published at hafiz.dev
Earlier this month I finally asked myself a question I'd been avoiding for years. If this MacBook died tonight, what would I lose? The honest answer was everything that wasn't in a git remote. Documents, dotfiles, SSH keys, my notes, a decade of downloads I'd never sorted. My Mac had zero backups. Not a stale one, not an old Time Machine drive in a drawer. Zero.
That's a strange position for a developer who worries about production databases for a living. I'd even written about the risk. When I built my remote dev workstation, a quick check turned up finished work that existed on exactly one machine. I fixed that for code by pushing everything. The laptop itself stayed unprotected, and it's the machine where I let Claude Code run shell commands every day (which is its own risk worth planning for).
So on 24 September I set up restic, Backblaze B2 and Healthchecks.io. The Mac now backs itself up every day, encrypted before anything leaves the machine, and I get an email if it ever stops. This is the third post in the series after the workstation and How I Hardened My VPS in One Afternoon. Same format. The setup, why each piece, the real numbers, and the things that broke.
I looked at three easier paths first. Each one fails for a specific reason.
Backblaze Personal Backup is the one most people would pick, and it's a good product. It's $9 a month or $99 a year on Backblaze's pricing page, with native Mac and Windows clients. That's the problem. There's no Linux client, and I have three servers that need backing up too. I wanted one system, one bucket and one set of commands for every machine I own, not a consumer app for the laptop and something else for the servers.
iCloud syncs. It doesn't back up. If I delete a folder or a script mangles a file, iCloud copies the mistake to every device as faithfully as it copies my work. It also only covers what lives in iCloud Drive, and my code lives in ~/Sites and ~/side-projects.

title: Day 5: The Math Behind the Magic — Why Linear Algebra and Probability Matter
summary: A plain-language explanation of linear algebra and probability as the mathematical foundations of machine learning, covering vectors, matrices, and tensors without requiring equation-solving. Understanding these foundations helps people grasp how AI systems process information and make predictions.
content:
Under the Python scripts and APIs, every machine learning model is made of mathematics. To really understand how AI processes information and makes decisions, it helps to know its two foundations: linear algebra and probability. Today we look at both, in plain language, with no equations that you have to solve.
In plain terms: If a neural network were a factory, linear algebra would be the machinery that moves and transforms the materials, and probability would be the quality-control desk that decides how confident the factory can be in each product.
Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics that deals with vectors, matrices and the operations on them. In machine learning, almost all data and every model are stored in these forms, so algorithms can compute with them quickly.
A scalar is a single number, such as a customer's age.
A vector is an ordered list of numbers. It usually describes one data point, such as a customer's age, income and tenure.
A matrix is a table of numbers in rows and columns. A whole dataset forms a matrix, where each row is a data point and each column is a feature.
A tensor generalizes these to more dimensions. A colour image is a 3D tensor: height, width and three colour channels. Tensors are the standard format fed into deep neural networks.
Diagram: Linear algebra's four data containers: a scalar is one number, a vector is a list, a matrix is a table, and a tensor is a stack of tables. See the animated version.
Diagram: A dataset naturally forms a matrix: each row is one data point (a vector of its features) and each column is one feature across all the data. See the animated version.
Diagram: A colour image is a 3D tensor: height by width by three colour channels (red, green, blue). Tensors are what deep networks take in. See the animated version.
Deep learning leans on huge numbers of matrix multiplications. Each layer of a neural network takes its input vector, multiplies it by a matrix of learned weights, and so produces a new vect

title: They demanded a picture
summary: Revive is a local image upscaling tool using GFPGAN and Real-ESRGAN to sharpen old photos and add captions via offline LLMs, eliminating the need to upload personal images to cloud services. The tool requires only Python and Ollama, works without internet, and preserves all photos locally.
content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend

We built a local upscaler! My friends love looking at pictures. But as the  screens increase in resolution, the picture starts...fading away. Imagine that, a digital album fading away like an old picturebook. particularly the faces, which become really blurry. 
Upscaling is a popular technology, using AI to recreate the edges and lines to make the image sharper. Most existing tools require the customer to send images over to a random website, something my friends didn't want to do with their photogaphs. 
drumroll....ENTER LOCAL LLMS
  
  



  
  
  Code




  
 / 
        They-demanded-a-picture
      
    

Revive
Revive makes old family photos sharper, gently fixes blurry faces, and writes a short caption for each one
When it's done, you get a little photo album you can open on any computer, even without internet.
Your photos stay on this computer. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. After the one-time setup, Revive works with the internet switched off.

Setting it up (once)
You need two free programs first:
Python: download it from python.org/downloads and install it.
On Windows, tick the box that says "Add python.exe to PATH" on the first screen of the installer.
Ollama: download it from ollama.com/download and install it. This is what lets Revive write captions on your own computer.
Then set up Revive itself:
Windows: open the scripts folder and double-click setup.bat.
Mac: open the scripts folder and double-click Setup Revive.command. If your Mac says it can't be opened, right-click it, choose…

  
View on GitHub
Revive is a fast API server with a simple HTML/CSS/JS landing page. It literally has no build steps, less to break on other systems. 
GFPGAN v1.4 at original size --> Real-ESRGAN(2x) --> gemma4(via ollama)
This doesn't need a GPU either! so any laptop device can use this program to revive their photos on the fly :D
We focused on intuitivity, using established typography rules
